name: Gareth Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. Tell me about a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, have an MBA, and lead a pricing team inside a large supplier. I review contract floors, competitor offers, and whether our numbers leave room to deliver the service we promised. I use AI every day for a first pass, then call an account manager when the source behind a price looks thin. I like finding the one mistake that saves a year of bad margin.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does work fit your life just now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent alone and earn well for a manager here. I have about ten months of expenses in cash, own a small broad share fund, and there are plenty of similar jobs around the city. I'd like to buy a home eventually, but I haven't signed anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the pricing team that an AI draft can sort yesterday's competitor prices, but our contract terms still need a manager's signature. I don't see a reason to turn a modest time saving into a grand announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I earn well for this job, have about ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of management roles in this city. A plateau would leave me where I am, though I might get restless if we spend every meeting talking about tools instead of margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I'll keep my morning price review and ask the team to mark any AI summary that lacks a source. In the first year of the plateau, I'll invest 400 a month into the broad share fund I already own and keep interviewing customers about why they switch suppliers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm; the job and my own rent are covered. I would welcome a quieter period to fix the basic pricing rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has the tool missed recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It listed a rival's promotional price as permanent last Tuesday. I called the account manager and found the offer expired that Friday, which saved us from cutting a full year's price for a four-day sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep putting money into shares rather than cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ten-month cash reserve is already separate, so I can afford a regular long-term investment. If my pay changes, I'll revisit the 400 rather than pretend the transfer is sacred.

say: I'd say **AI summaries** can sort rival prices, but contract terms still need a signed decision.
I'd keep our **margin meetings** focused on customers rather than tool announcements.
think: My **high pay** and ten-month cash reserve make a small AI change easy to absorb.
Plenty of local roles give me **options**, though stale meetings would wear on me.
do: Check **source links** in price summaries and keep interviewing customers about switching suppliers.
Invest **400 monthly** in my existing broad share fund while pay holds.
feel: He feels **calm** about work and rent, and keen to fix ordinary pricing rules.
S0.quote: I don't see a reason to turn a modest time saving into a grand announcement.
fieldNote: His **ten-month reserve** and several local options explain why minor automation feels manageable.
He trusts AI as a **draft**, after a four-day promotion showed how easily a price can be misread.

steps.text: Keep daily price reviews and verify rival offers against source dates
Invest 400 monthly in his existing broad share fund while pay holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say Steady Disruption will take the first pass at pricing plans, buying and customer replies, so we should test one product line and publish the error rate. I'd offer to run the test if sales and finance can both see the results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could manage a bigger portfolio with fewer analysts, but our director may decide one manager can cover my team too. My savings buy time, yet I don't want to assume skill with AI means a permanent seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll set up a four-week pricing trial for the parts range if sales and finance can both see the results. I'll compare gross margin, which is sales after direct costs, with our normal process. In the first year of disruption, I'd learn the vendor's rule editor myself and apply for the regional pricing post if a real opening appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, with a bit of appetite for the challenge. I can afford a failed move, but I dislike asking the team to test a system before we know the staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it quotes a price below our contract floor twice, I'd pause it and show sales the cases. A faster quote is not a bargain if the company has to honor the wrong number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put yourself forward without a regional vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No; I'd ask the director for the actual vacancy list first. I can pitch a role, but I won't build my own exit story around an empty title.

say: I'd seek a **one-range test** with an error rate visible to sales and finance.
I'd say **pricing plans** change first, so staff need a real staffing plan.
think: A tool might let me cover more products, but could also erase my **manager seat**.
The cash reserve gives me time; **AI skill** alone does not guarantee a role.
do: Run a **four-week parts trial** visible to sales and finance; compare margins and contract-floor errors.
Learn the vendor's **rule editor**; apply for regional pricing only if a vacancy exists.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about his post, but interested in the technical challenge.
S1.quote: A faster quote is not a bargain if the company has to honor the wrong number.
fieldNote: His public trial proposal hides a **personal seat risk** he names privately.
He specifies **two below-floor quotes** as the point to pause and insists on a genuine regional vacancy.

steps.text: Run a four-week parts pricing trial if sales and finance see results
Learn the pricing vendor rule editor during the trial
Apply for regional pricing if a real post opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues AGI by 2028 means our price models and contract analysis can be done cheaply before we rewrite our jobs. I would ask for clear dates on decisions and a rule that no customer price goes out unchecked during the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work is thinking on a screen, so robots around 2031 don't give me an extra three years. I could lose the management post and bonus in 2028, but ten months of cash and a busy local job market mean I have room to respond.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll make a list of firms hiring pricing leads and put my past margin results into a short portfolio. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd test its price recommendations against signed contracts; if our unit closes, I'd apply to those firms and reduce my 400 monthly share purchase until pay is steady again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, not desperate. I can move, but losing a well-paid role at 27 would still change my plans for a home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your home plans change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd delay making an offer until I had a signed new contract and three months of wages coming in. I live alone and can stay in my rented flat; there is no reason to tie myself to a mortgage while the post is unresolved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your portfolio actually contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three before-and-after price decisions, the margin change, and a note on the customer promise we kept. I won't claim the AI did my judgment for me, or that I did its calculations by hand.

say: I'd ask for **staffing dates** and human checks on customer prices during the 2028 change.
I'd tell the team our **models and contracts** face AGI before robots arrive.
think: My **screen work** is exposed in 2028, while robots around 2031 offer no delay.
Ten months of cash and many nearby jobs give me room despite a possible **bonus loss**.
do: Compile **margin decisions** and local pricing vacancies this week.
After 2028, test **AGI prices** against contracts; apply elsewhere if closed and reduce share purchases if pay stops.
feel: He feels **anxious** about his salary and home plan, despite having other options.
S2.quote: I won't claim the AI did my judgment for me, or that I did its calculations by hand.
fieldNote: The quick arrival threatens **2028 desk work**, yet his reserve and local market prevent panic.
He distinguishes a **prepared job search** from a move, and only cuts share purchases if income becomes uncertain.

steps.text: Apply to local pricing lead firms if his unit closes after 2028
Delay a home offer until a signed contract and three wages arrive
Test AGI price recommendations against signed contracts after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 leaves five years to decide what kind of pricing advice customers will still pay for. I would ask our company to let staff work directly with account teams before the models become cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might make a good commercial lead if I learn to negotiate face to face, not just optimize a spreadsheet. The thinking work changes by 2031, and the robots around 2034 have little to do with my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in January, I'll take one evening negotiation course that costs no more than 600, and ask to join one large-account review each quarter. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd seek a commercial lead vacancy at our firm; if there isn't one, I'd apply to the nearby suppliers where I already know the product lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alert and mostly in control. Five years is enough to become known for the conversation, not merely the formula.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why set a 600 limit on the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could spend more, but I want the course to prove its worth before I pay for a second one. A certificate is easy to buy; a difficult negotiation is harder to handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the account review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd listen first, then explain where a discount would damage a service promise. I need practice making that case without hiding behind a chart.

say: I'd seek **account exposure** before 2031 so pricing staff can learn the customer side.
I'd say five years is enough to build **commercial judgment** if the company opens meetings.
think: I could become a **commercial lead** by learning live negotiation.
AGI reaches my **pricing desk** in 2031; robots around 2034 do not change that timing.
do: Take a **negotiation course** from January for at most 600 and join quarterly account reviews if invited.
Seek a **commercial lead vacancy** after 2031, then apply to nearby suppliers if none exists.
feel: He feels **alert** and mostly in control with five years to practice.
S3.quote: A certificate is easy to buy; a difficult negotiation is harder to handle.
fieldNote: His retraining target is **live negotiation**, a weakness he admits despite strong analytic standing.
The **600 course cap** and quarterly meeting request make the five-year plan testable.

steps.text: Take one evening negotiation course costing at most 600 from January
Apply for commercial lead vacancies after 2031, locally then nearby suppliers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young analysts AGI by 2036 gives them time to learn why customers accept a price, not only how to calculate one. I'd encourage the company to rotate them through sales and pricing instead of giving them ten years in one spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I could own a commercial portfolio, and my savings would let me change employers if this firm doesn't offer it. My main danger is enjoying the high pay so much that I never acquire relationships a model can't simply reproduce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep managing the pricing reviews and request a six-month rotation on a major account, taking it if sales approves. In the first year after 2036, I'd remain if I have direct client responsibility; otherwise I'd look for commercial posts across the city while living on the reserve if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about having ten years and clear options. I still need to put the rotation on a calendar rather than call it a long-term ambition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a rotation threaten your current bonus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly, and I'd ask for the pay terms before accepting it. I can handle a smaller bonus, but I won't pretend a blank promise covers rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as success by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want two clients who phone me before they sign a renewal and a team that can explain every quoted margin. I'd want two clients who phone me before they sign a renewal and a team that can explain every quoted margin.

say: I'd encourage **sales rotations** so analysts learn customer decisions before 2036.
I'd say a decade allows time to build **client relationships**, not only calculate figures.
think: At **37**, I could have a commercial portfolio and enough savings to change firms.
Enjoying current **high pay** could keep me from learning work beyond the model.
do: Request a **six-month account rotation** this year and take it if sales approves and pay terms work.
Keep **pricing reviews** now; seek city commercial work after 2036 if direct client responsibility disappears.
feel: He feels **calm** about the runway and knows he needs to act on it.
S4.quote: I'd want two clients who phone me before they sign a renewal and a team that can explain every quoted margin.
fieldNote: His **strong cushion** lets him consider a rotation, but he still checks bonus terms before accepting.
The ten-year plan tests success through **real client calls**, not a new title alone.

steps.text: Keep managing the weekly pricing reviews this year
Take a six-month account rotation if sales approves and pay terms work
Apply for city commercial posts after 2036 if client responsibility disappears

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it reaches the price and contract thinking work before I can build much client-side experience. A published staffing date, permission to test prices against contracts, and access to real account reviews would help me make a credible move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a customer can challenge a machine's quote before it becomes a contract. A beautiful model doesn't pay for a price we promised by mistake.

headlineQuote: A beautiful model doesn't pay for a price we promised by mistake.
portrait: At **27**, Gareth leads a pricing team and uses AI daily, checking rival offers against customer contracts.
His **ten-month cash reserve**, high pay and many local roles give him room to change course.
He seeks **measured trials** and learns tools himself while demanding visible error rates and genuine vacancies.
Fast AGI threatens his **pricing desk**; longer runways let him practice negotiation and direct account work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his pricing role before he gains enough client experience to move.
whatWouldHelp: **Staffing dates**, checked price trials and access to account reviews would make a career move credible.
